overview: The map’s Simhala label covers Sri Lanka from about 500 BCE to 800 CE, a span of changing rulers and regional communities. Anuradhapura became a major capital and Buddhist center. Its island-shaped outline is not proof that one state controlled every district throughout these centuries; neither endpoint marks the beginning or disappearance of Sri Lankan civilization.

periods.title: An expanding early city
periods.summary: Anuradhapura grew within trading networks before the famous third-century BCE Buddhist missions.

periods.title: Buddhist institutions and royal monuments
periods.summary: Sacred traditions connect Mahinda and Sanghamitta with Buddhism’s expansion; royal patrons built enduring religious monuments.

periods.title: Rival monasteries and overseas connections
periods.summary: Mahasena’s patronage changed the balance between major monasteries; later rulers supported their coexistence.

periods.title: Kashyapa’s Sigiriya court
periods.summary: Kashyapa established his court at Sigiriya; after his defeat, the complex returned to monastic use.

periods.title: Continuing kingdoms and skilled production
periods.summary: Anuradhapura continued, while island communities sustained farming and specialized industries, including wind-powered iron production.

items.text: Anuradhapura’s history lies in layers of rebuilt buildings and discarded objects. A trench only ten meters square descended through roughly ten meters of deposits. Excavations show an urban settlement and trade networks already developing before the third-century BCE missions traditionally associated with Ashoka.

Buddhist tradition remembers the nun Sanghamitta bringing a cutting of the Bodhi tree from India in the third century BCE. The tree became a living focus of pilgrimage at Anuradhapura, connecting generations of worshippers with the story of the Buddha’s enlightenment.

The second-century BCE king Dutthagamani was remembered for monumental building, including the Ruvanvelisaya stupa and the Brazen Palace. Anuradhapura’s huge stupas made sacred relics visible in the cityscape: rounded monuments set on circular foundations, sometimes surrounded by rings of stone columns.

Royal support could divide monasteries as well as enrich them. Around the late third century, Mahasena withdrew support from the Mahavihara and founded Jetavana; materials from Mahavihara were taken for Abhayagiri. His son restored relations, and all three communities continued receiving patronage.

Between 477 and 495, Kashyapa made Sigiriya his royal stronghold amid a struggle with his brother Moggallana. Palaces, gardens and defenses transformed the rock and its surroundings. Kashyapa’s defeat ended this brief royal episode; the place subsequently served Buddhist monastic life again.

Reservoirs, often called tanks, stored water for dry-zone farming. Their history includes local chiefs, families, individual owners and royal patrons. An inscription might donate part of a tank’s income or water rights to a monastery, rather than hand over every field and every drop.

Water management required people with practical responsibilities. Second-century BCE inscriptions name a flow operator, a canal officer and an irrigation officer. Their precise job descriptions have not survived, but the titles show that directing water was organized work, not simply a king ordering a lake into existence.

A woman named Anulabi, daughter of Mitaya, appears in a roughly third-century rock inscription. She gave income from a share of her family’s reservoir to monks at Gagapavata. This unusually personal record shows family property and a woman making a substantial religious gift.

Some excavated bowls have shallow bodies, wide mouths and scratched interiors. Archaeologists compare them with the nambiliya, a bowl used to separate grit from rice. Examples in early settlements around Anuradhapura bring food preparation into view: someone still had to keep unwanted crunch out of dinner.

Another rock inscription, assigned to the fifth or sixth century, records a family’s effort to overcome slavery. Aba’s elder brother paid one hundred kahavanas to secure Aba’s freedom. The payment and the hope that it would earn religious merit are preserved; the brothers’ wider life stories are not.

sections.title: Learning, festivals and a visitor far from home

items.text: The Chinese monk Faxian visited in the early fifth century. At Abhayagiri, the sight of a merchant offering a white silk fan brought him to tears after years away from familiar people and places. His account preserves homesickness beside descriptions of spectacular religious buildings.

Faxian describes preaching halls at four important streets. On designated days, people laid out carpets and raised a pulpit; monks and lay listeners gathered to hear teaching. Learning could happen through a public spoken gathering, rather than only through reading a manuscript.

During his two-year stay, Faxian obtained Buddhist disciplinary and scriptural texts unavailable in China. He carried them away by sea. When a storm threatened the ship, he feared the merchants would throw his books overboard with the cargo: a scholar’s luggage could be precious indeed.

For the tooth-relic festival, Faxian reports an announcement made from an elephant ten days ahead. The route displayed scenes from the Buddha’s past lives; devotees brought flowers and incense and lit lamps. Processions brought religion into shared streets and involved far more people than the clergy.

A chronicle credits King Upatissa I, in the fourth to early fifth century, with establishing maternity homes. This is literary evidence for care around childbirth. Surviving hospital ruins often belong to later centuries, so their detailed floor plans cannot simply be assigned to his reign.

Toilet engineering also survives at Abhayagiri, although the study does not securely date these particular structures before 800. Clay pipes led urine into stacks of bottomless pots, with traces suggesting sand, lime and charcoal filters. It is a revealing comparison from Anuradhapura’s longer history, not a model of every household bathroom.

The chronicles also credit the eighth-century king Aggabodhi VII with investigating medicinal plants and their effectiveness. In this account, royal concern for health extended beyond paying for buildings: it included curiosity about what remedies could do.

At Samanalawewa, ironworkers placed furnaces where monsoon winds could supply air to the fire. Archaeologists found evidence reaching back to the seventh century. Replica experiments produced high-carbon steel, demonstrating a sophisticated process in which careful furnace design made seasonal winds part of the workshop.

Sigiriya’s water gardens linked pools and fountains through underground conduits. Circular limestone plates formed fountain outlets, and some fountains still work when rainfall supplies sufficient water. The spectacle depended on engineering hidden beneath visitors’ feet, not just the beauty of the pools.

sections.title: Objects, art and a voice in writing

items.text: Pottery jars from Anuradhapura’s layers dated 300 to 600 held a chemical clue to distant trade. Their waterproof bitumen lining was traced to Susa in Iran. The jars carried liquids, but analysis did not identify the contents: their shape alone cannot tell us what anyone drank.

Sigiriya’s surviving paintings show richly adorned women, but their identities remain debated: royal figures, celestial beings and religious interpretations have all been proposed. Looking closely at the paintings reveals skill and courtly display; it does not establish that every pictured woman was one of Kashyapa’s wives.

Anulabi’s inscription lets us read a real personal introduction: “Mitayaha jita Anuḷabi,” meaning “Anulabi, daughter of Mitaya.” This is a scholarly Latin-letter transliteration of an inscription originally carved in Brahmi letters, dated approximately to the third century. The original letter shapes differ from modern Sinhala script.

ending.text: The map label stops at 800; Anuradhapura did not. Its later decline involved disrupted economic networks and political conflict, while other centers grew. Communities adapted, and Buddhist institutions, farming and Sri Lankan societies continued beyond this record’s boundaries.
